faq.q: What do these clothing ad templates include?
faq.a: You get the piece on an AI avatar, a spoken line, and a clip you can approve. A photo of a knit polo is enough to start.

faq.q: How does a clothing template become an ad?
faq.a: Put up a photo of a cardigan and name the shopper, for example someone buying a softer layer. The draft comes back as a clip you can post from this page.

faq.q: Which kinds of clothing can I start with?
faq.a: Start with a denim jacket, a dress, or a tailored trouser. The template is for a piece a person has on, so a folded stack is a weak source photo.

faq.q: Can I make several ads for one collection?
faq.a: Yes. The same trench can run once for a commute and again for a wet weekend, using the photo you already have. Shops with a long rack do this each time a new color lands.

faq.q: Which shops are these clothing templates built around?
faq.a: A shop that sells its own jackets and restocks through the month. The owner can run it, or someone on the marketing desk can.

faq.q: Can I use them if I have never edited a video?
faq.a: Yes. You supply the garment and say what the ad should claim. The template handles the avatar, the opening, and the cut. Earlier video experience is not required.

faq.q: After I upload a garment, when is the ad ready to post?
faq.a: The clip is ready to download once generation finishes. Take the file from this page and post the cut the shop already uses.

faq.q: What does a clothing ad cost, and can I post the square crop?
faq.a: A 6-second clip spends 24 credits, 10 seconds spends 40, 15 seconds spends 60, and 30 seconds spends 120. A still from the same garment spends 24 credits. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600. The screen shows that cost before you start. The download has no watermark. Notes on the square crop are on [AI Instagram ads](page:plat-instagram).

faq.q: Can my shop send garments in from its own system?
faq.a: Yes. An API connection can send a garment from your catalog and bring the finished ad back. A failed job returns its credits.

items.t: New jacket on the product page
items.d: The shop uploads the hanger photo when the carton arrives and places the on-model frame beside the flat lay. Hem, sleeves and pockets are checked against the physical jacket before the listing goes up.

items.t: One standing scene for the launch
items.d: The boutique picks a single standing scene for the main photo of a new dress. Neckline, color, and how it fastens are compared with the garment on the rail before anyone posts it.

items.t: A back view from a second source
items.d: The label uses a photo of the back so the collar and rear seams can show. That second file is its own run, and the cost is shown before it starts.
The agency repeats upload, scene and download for each clothing client. People in the frames are generated. They are not hired models and not customers.

They pick a generated person for the jacket instead of booking a model. Collar, hem, and color are checked against the garment.
